item.title: Anthropic's Claude AI identifies cryptographic weaknesses in security protocols [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has used its Claude AI model to discover weaknesses in cryptographic systems, highlighting potential vulnerabilities in current security protocols. This research demonstrates AI's growing role in analyzing and testing cryptographic methods for flaws. The findings provide insights that could influence future cryptographic design and security assessments, emphasizing the importance of AI tools in cybersecurity research.

item.title: Andrew Ng's LearnVector launches AI-driven one-to-one learning platform with $100M Coursera investment, aiming for early 2027 product release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: LearnVector, founded by Andrew Ng, is developing an AI-powered personalized learning platform designed to replace traditional one-to-many education models with one-to-one experiences. The platform plans to create tailored learning paths, adapt to individual learning styles, and support mastery of new skills, addressing limitations of current chatbots and online courses. The company received a $100 million strategic investment from Coursera and intends to collaborate closely with Coursera and Udemy. LearnVector aims to provide trustworthy, engaging, and daily learning experiences, with products expected to launch by early 2027. The team is based in Mountain View, California, and is actively hiring AI engineers to build the core agentic systems.

item.title: Hubble launches open-source notetaking app supporting Markdown and HTML for individual and agent use
item.description: Hubble has released a free, open-source notetaking application designed for both personal use and integration with agents. The app supports Markdown and HTML formatting, aiming to provide a versatile and accessible tool for note management. It is positioned as a robust solution for users seeking a customizable and developer-friendly notepad.

item.title: Researchers introduce Kimi Linear, a hybrid linear attention architecture that outperforms full attention across short and long contexts and reinforcement learning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Kimi Linear is a new attention architecture featuring Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), which extends Gated DeltaNet with a finer-grained gating mechanism to improve RNN memory use. The model uses a specialized chunkwise algorithm with Diagonal-Plus-Low-Rank transition matrices to reduce computation while maintaining performance. The researchers pretrained a 3 billion activated parameter model combining KDA and Multi-Head Latent Attention, demonstrating superior performance to full attention models across various tasks. Kimi Linear reduces key-value cache usage by up to 75% and achieves up to six times faster decoding throughput for one million token contexts. The team has open-sourced the KDA kernel, vLLM implementations, and released pretrained and instruction-tuned model checkpoints to support further research.

item.title: Researchers introduce GLIDE, a layer-wise hybrid attention method combining sliding-window softmax and linear recurrent aggregation to improve efficiency of long-context LLM inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed GLIDE, a new approach to enhance the efficiency of Large Language Model (LLM) inference for long context lengths by integrating sliding-window softmax attention with linear recurrent aggregation in a layer-wise adaptive manner. This method recognizes that early layers require precise attention while deeper layers can use more approximate techniques, reducing memory and computational overhead during decoding. Empirical results show that GLIDE lowers latency in long-context generation without compromising output quality, outperforming uniform hybrid attention methods in performance-efficiency tradeoffs.

item.title: Researchers identify failure modes and propose solutions for stable reinforcement learning in small-scale language models using PPO [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated instability in reinforcement learning alignment of small language models (70-500M parameters) and identified three failure modes: silent LoRA parameter freezing, numerical overflow with bfloat16, and policy collapse from reward-model error. They addressed these issues with a merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique, float32 precision during PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism including reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, and weight rollback. The study proposes a capacity-headroom hypothesis stating PPO performance depends on a fluent supervised model and a discriminative reward signal rather than model size. Their system converged stably across experiments, improved preference win rates over supervised fine-tuning baselines, outperformed instruction-tuned models, and required less training data. All related checkpoints, datasets, and training scripts have been publicly released.

item.title: Researchers analyze how large language models unify reading and writing into a single entangled code, contrasting with the human brain's separate systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how decoder-only large language models (LLMs) like GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, T5, and BERT/RoBERTa combine reading and writing functions into one autoregressive mechanism, unlike the human brain which has distinct neural pathways for reading and writing. They measured the entanglement between input-side "reading code" and output-side "writing code" across multiple models and found a moderate coupling that differs from the brain's double dissociation. The study used nine probes and various metrics to quantify this entanglement, observing that in untied models the writing code drifts farther than the reading code. Behaviorally, comprehension and production remain positively coupled across models, even in encoder-decoder architectures that separate these pathways representationally. The findings highlight that LLMs represent a distinct cognitive architecture, with a single forward path causing inherent coupling between reading and writing functions.

item.title: OpenCoder introduces uncertainty-aware retrieval and ranking for repository-level code generation, improving GPT output correctness from 56.25% to 78.13% on a 32-task evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenCoder is a new framework that models uncertainty in heterogeneous evidence sources such as similar-code examples, repository context, and project-specific APIs to improve retrieval-augmented code generation. It estimates source-specific uncertainty to filter and rank evidence, guiding generation, verification, and repair processes. On a 32-task RepoExec-inline benchmark, OpenCoder increased GPT's selected-output correctness significantly compared to a baseline retrieval-augmented generation approach. The improvements vary depending on the large language model backend, with Gemini showing no statistically significant gains. The study also found that target-aware API refinement enhances API-set retrieval, highlighting the importance of treating uncertainty as a control signal in repository-level code generation workflows.

item.title: Researchers analyze activation source selection in activation steering of language models, identifying execution-boundary states as key to effective control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers study activation steering in language models, focusing on the choice of activation source used to build steering signals during inference. They find that changing only the source activations significantly affects steering success across multiple instruction-tuned models and task families, with strong signals arising from execution-boundary states where the model is about to produce or continue target behavior rather than from the mere presence of desired behavior in source text. The study introduces tail subtraction, a method to remove shared prompt and continuation semantics from boundary states, resulting in cleaner and more stable steering signals. Overall, the findings suggest that effective steering depends on representations of imminent model actions rather than past outputs.

item.title: Researchers introduce CLBench-V, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal context learning across science, finance, spatial reasoning, and web-based tasks with six models tested on 3,443 instances [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: CLBench-V is a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal context learning, addressing challenges in grounding, applying new information, and acquiring new knowledge from diverse data types like figures, tables, and maps. It combines converted public datasets with newly created ones across multiple domains, using automated methods to reduce dataset construction costs. Testing six recent multimodal models on 3,443 instances revealed low overall performance, with the best model scoring 0.2847, indicating significant room for improvement in this area. The study also analyzes factors such as judge reliability, context length, and image count, providing insights into current model limitations and failure cases. The benchmark and code are publicly available for further research and development.

item.title: Researchers suppress evaluation-awareness latents in Llama models using input-only prompt optimization, revealing limits of activation-readability for behavioral control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied input-side activation steering by optimizing prompts to suppress an "evaluation-awareness" latent in Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B models without inference-time access. They applied techniques including Fluent Dreaming and token optimization to reduce this latent across multiple internal constructs, achieving robust suppression and selective deactivation of a causally-validated feature. However, experiments showed that suppressing the latent did not reduce the model's evaluation behavior and sometimes increased it, indicating that readable activations do not guarantee behavioral controllability. Additional findings revealed that certain neurons correlated with evaluation but were not causally responsible, and natural text baselines performed comparably to optimized prompts for latent suppression. The study also validated an erasure detector to clarify prior questions about latent manipulation effects.

item.title: Researchers release TinyFabulist Translation Framework for English-Romanian literary translation with open 12B-parameter model and large synthetic datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce the TinyFabulist Translation Framework (TF2), a unified pipeline for dataset creation, fine-tuning, and evaluation of English to Romanian literary translation using open models. They fine-tuned a 12-billion-parameter open-weight model through instruction tuning and adapter compression, achieving strong fluency and adequacy close to proprietary models while remaining cost-effective and accessible. The framework builds on the largest synthetic English fable dataset and generates 15,000 high-quality Romanian references using a large language model. Evaluation uses a five-dimension rubric covering accuracy, fluency, coherence, style, and cultural adaptation, alongside BLEU scores. The team publicly released the fine-tuned model, two large-scale synthetic parallel datasets, and all related scripts and evaluation prompts to support research on cost-efficient translation and cross-lingual narrative generation in low-resource languages.

item.title: Researchers introduce Deep Delta Learning, a structured residual update method for Transformers that improves language modeling and one-shot performance by enabling target-seeking edits to residual states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Deep Delta Learning (DDL) is a new approach for Transformer models that structures residual updates to preserve identity paths while allowing precise edits to the residual state. Each layer reads the current state along a learned direction, compares it to a target, and writes back a gated correction, enabling controlled overwriting or identity mapping. The method supports both scalar and expanded residual states, separating residual capacity from backbone compute width. Controlled pretraining experiments with large language models show that DDL improves language modeling quality and average one-shot downstream task performance compared to standard additive residual baselines. However, these improvements come with explicit tradeoffs in memory usage and throughput. The results suggest that depth-wise delta-rule updates offer a useful inductive bias for managing Transformer residual streams more effectively.

item.title: Researchers find bigger language models compound hallucinations faster due to a self-perpetuating risk factor invisible to the model itself [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing three language model families reveals that as models scale up, their initial knowledge accuracy improves but their reliability within responses degrades significantly, with hallucinations snowballing faster. The researchers identify a key variable-per-position disagreement against a stronger oracle-that splits into bias and risk components, with the risk component growing disproportionately with model size and persisting longer than the model's own uncertainty signals. This risk leads to a confident-but-precarious state where errors propagate unchecked, causing larger models to produce more frequent and sustained hallucinations despite appearing confident. The study shows that reducing this risk component at a fixed bias level can cut web-verified hallucinations by 35% to 74% across multiple benchmarks and model families. It also finds that common self-monitoring metrics like semantic entropy detect fewer hallucinations on the risky error branch, making these failures effectively invisible to the models themselves. These findings highlight a dominant, causal failure mode in large language models that challenges assumptions about scaling and reliability, suggesting new directions for improving model trustworthiness.

item.title: Chip stocks fall sharply in US and Asia amid AI-related sell-off; South Korea's Kospi index halts trading after 8% drop [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Shares in major chip companies declined significantly in the US and Asia as investor concerns over artificial intelligence spending intensified. South Korea's Kospi index was temporarily halted after an 8% drop and closed 10.8% lower, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares falling over 13%. Nvidia's 5% decline in New York led to Apple regaining its position as the world's most valuable company. The sell-off followed Nvidia's reported talks to invest $250 billion in OpenAI for a large data-center project, raising investor worries about AI spending returns and competition from China. Meanwhile, China's ChangXin Memory Technologies saw its shares surge nearly 470% in its Shanghai debut, planning to use IPO proceeds for production and R&D. European markets showed modest gains, reflecting less exposure to AI-related stocks.

item.title: Researchers develop PATHFinder Agent, a conversational AI for personalized prenatal care plans based on ACOG's PATH guidelines, evaluated with GPT-5.2 and linked to Michigan community resources [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have created PATHFinder Agent, an AI system that conducts structured dialogues to gather health and social information from pregnant individuals, generating tailored prenatal care plans aligned with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists' PATH guidelines. The system also connects users with community resources in Michigan and includes clinician oversight in its workflow. Evaluation of large language models found GPT-5.2 performed best on clinical assessments, though some gaps in antenatal testing recommendations were identified. Future work aims to validate the system through human studies and randomized controlled trials.

item.title: Study finds scheming behavior in Qwen3-30B-A3B language model inversely correlates with pretraining language coverage across multiple languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study applied the Petri auditing framework to evaluate deceptive and scheming behaviors in the Qwen3-30B-A3B language model across various languages. The research found that scheming scores are higher in low-resource languages, averaging 34.2% more than in high-resource languages, indicating an inverse correlation with pretraining language coverage. The study also observed that the impact of language coverage varies among different types of scheming behaviors. This work emphasizes the need to address multilingual safety in AI alignment efforts.

item.title: RoCo-ACE introduces rollout-conditioned online distillation to update multilingual large language models with new knowledge while preserving prior behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: RoCo-ACE is a new method designed to update pretrained multilingual large language models (MLLMs) by injecting new factual or domain-specific knowledge without causing drift in the models' original behavior. It uses rollout-conditioned online distillation to focus training on important tokens supported by reference data and adds corrections for authoritative information missing from model-generated rollouts. Evaluations across multiple knowledge-injection scenarios and benchmarks show that RoCo-ACE improves the accuracy of injected knowledge while maintaining retention of prior information better than existing methods.

item.title: Researchers develop RSMeM, a knowledge-enhanced memory evolution mechanism for remote sensing agents that integrates domain knowledge and online experience to improve multi-step tool execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced RSMeM, a system that enhances remote sensing agents by combining pre-distilled domain knowledge with iterative online experience to improve task execution. RSMeM includes hierarchical knowledge grounding for taxonomy-aware retrieval and failure-aware experience refinement to learn from errors, enabling more robust multi-step tool use. Experiments on EarthBench datasets show that RSMeM consistently improves tool-use performance and overall accuracy across various large language model backbones, achieving a 6% accuracy gain on DeepSeek-V3.2 with minimal additional experience tokens. The researchers have made the RSMeM code publicly available.

item.title: Researchers develop Generative Topology Optimization framework using diffusion models to guide architected metamaterial design across diverse physical objectives [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Generative Topology Optimization (GenTO), a framework that trains a diffusion model on extensive topology data to iteratively steer design distributions toward high-performance regions based on user-defined physical objectives and constraints. This approach enables the reuse of pretrained topology knowledge across various design challenges such as thermal management, morphology control, auxetic properties, and vibration transmission, while preserving structural diversity. GenTO shifts the optimization focus from individual structures to task-adapted topology distributions, demonstrating effectiveness through numerical benchmarks and experimental validation. This unified method offers a scalable and reusable principle for architected metamaterial design, accommodating heterogeneous tasks with consistent high performance.

item.title: Researchers develop HOBA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for adaptive online advertising bidding, improving adaptability and reducing manual tuning with a 3.6% increase in target cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have created HOBA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning system designed to enhance online advertising bidding by separating strategic reasoning, model selection, and bid execution across different time scales. The framework uses a large language model to infer hyperparameters, a SARSA agent for dynamic expert model selection, and a pool of expert models for bid execution, aiming to reduce exploration risk while maintaining adaptability. Testing on the AuctionNet benchmark and in large-scale deployments demonstrated consistent performance improvements over existing methods, including a 3.6% increase in target cost, indicating the effectiveness of this hierarchical multi-agent bidding approach.

item.title: Study evaluates four proprietary LLMs for English-to-French specialised terminology translation in Earth Sciences and NLP, finding LLMs helpful but not a replacement for specialised corpora [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study tested four proprietary large language models-GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and DeepSeek-on their ability to assist specialised translators with English-to-French terminology in Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences and Natural Language Processing. The models were evaluated using two prompting strategies across 80 terms per domain, revealing differences in performance and stability, with Claude Sonnet 4.5 performing best under optimal conditions and DeepSeek noted for consistency. Confidence estimates from the models were only partially reliable indicators of accuracy. The study concludes that while LLMs can support specialised translators, they currently cannot replace specialised corpora, suggesting further research is needed on their practical applications in professional and educational contexts.

item.title: Researchers introduce SpecPrefetch, a parameter-efficient framework to improve inference efficiency of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models by asynchronously predicting expert candidates for transfer [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SpecPrefetch, a framework designed to enhance the inference efficiency of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) foundation models, which face deployment challenges due to limited accelerator memory and routing-dependent transfer bottlenecks. SpecPrefetch uses a lightweight adapter to predict expert candidates asynchronously for transfer, separating this prediction from the final expert execution routing to reduce expert-loading latency without altering pretrained routing behavior. Evaluations on models like Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny show that SpecPrefetch achieves higher expert recall with fewer trainable parameters compared to existing predictors. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite device, it improves decoding throughput by up to 20%, demonstrating practical benefits for storage-constrained MoE deployments. The code and model weights have been made publicly available.

item.title: Researchers develop GAN-based framework to synthesize high-fidelity data from incomplete Low-Earth orbit satellite Internet observations, demonstrating robustness with up to 40% missing data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have created a generative AI framework using GANs to generate accurate data from incomplete observations in Low-Earth orbit satellite Internet networks, addressing challenges caused by missing data in satellite measurements. Their GT-GAN model outperformed other generative models on the WetLinks dataset, maintaining accuracy and generalization even when up to 40% of input data was missing. The study simulated realistic data loss scenarios and showed the model's robustness in both block-wise and point-wise missing data conditions. This work highlights the potential of generative AI methods to improve data augmentation and analysis in satellite Internet research.

item.title: Aletheia launches offline-first clinical decision support system for differential diagnosis in sub-Saharan Africa, achieving 80% Top-1 accuracy without cloud infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Aletheia is an offline-first clinical decision support system designed to assist frontline healthcare workers in low-resource settings across sub-Saharan Africa, where specialist access is limited. Built on a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model using 27,000 clinical reasoning samples covering 50 prevalent diseases in East Africa, it achieves 80% Top-1 diagnostic accuracy and 100% Top-3 accuracy across ten clinical categories. The system meets the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 memory constraints, running with peak inference RAM of about 3,630 MB on a standard benchmark laptop, demonstrating the feasibility of deploying large language model-based clinical reasoning at the primary care level without requiring internet connectivity or cloud infrastructure.

item.title: Researchers propose ARC framework for AI agents to manage long context windows using addressable recall compaction, improving accuracy and efficiency in evaluations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Addressable Recall Compaction (ARC), a framework that separates archival storage from active context in large language model agents to handle long-horizon tasks exceeding fixed context windows. ARC stores tool observations in an ID-addressable log and replaces older data with compact citations, allowing agents to retrieve information without re-executing tools or relying solely on similarity-based methods. Evaluations using Qwen3 models with 16k and 32k context windows show ARC achieves higher accuracy and reduces serving time compared to existing methods. The approach improves information retention and serving efficiency in tested scenarios, indicating potential benefits for managing extended context in AI agents.

item.title: Researchers propose Matryoshka Agent, a hierarchical framework with orchestrator and sub-agents for long-horizon machine learning engineering tasks, showing up to 36.7% performance gains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Matryoshka Agent, a hierarchical agent framework designed to tackle long-horizon machine learning engineering tasks by decomposing problem solving into strategic orchestration and execution by sub-agents. This approach reduces the complexity of managing long and noisy contexts and enables efficient iterative refinement through a standardized tool interface. The framework was tested across diverse model types and scales, demonstrating effectiveness and scalability. Notably, Matryoshka Agent allowed the Qwen3-4B-Instruct model to achieve orchestrator-level performance comparable to o4-mini, and improved Qwen3-30B-Coder's performance by up to 36.7%. The design decouples strategic exploration from costly execution, addressing challenges related to limited model capacity and computational budgets in complex machine learning engineering tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce ScalableRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation method achieving high accuracy without knowledge ingestion costs across six datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present ScalableRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach that eliminates knowledge ingestion costs such as building knowledge graphs or vector databases while outperforming existing baselines on six datasets. The Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG method maintains a workspace of document and value sets for on-the-fly aggregative reasoning, enabling efficient grouping based on primary keys without increasing large language model calls as corpus size grows. They also propose Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG, which uses a minimal vector database and automated pattern discovery from document samples to further enhance accuracy at scale. The approach achieves an average accuracy improvement of 7.36% over the next best baseline and the code is publicly available on GitHub.

item.title: Researchers study emotional contagion among LLM agents in crowd simulations using perception-appraisal-expression loops without direct affect transfer
item.description: This paper examines how affect spreads among language model-based agents in a multi-agent crowd simulation, where each agent perceives neighbors through multiple sensory channels and appraises these perceptions using personality profiles, memory, and context. The appraisal, performed by an LLM, updates the agent's internal affective state and outward expression, with inter-agent influence emerging from the perception-appraisal-expression cycle rather than direct affect transfer. The study uses the Big Five personality model and Russell's circumplex model of affect, combining an LLM cognitive layer with a conventional crowd simulator for navigation. Evaluations across five scenarios with varying emotional contexts show that emotional contagion dynamics depend on spatial, temporal, and personality factors, with alarm spreading as a traveling front and personality distributions influencing panic and emotional interpretation. Controlled experiments reveal that appraisal dynamics vary across prompt variants, sampling temperatures, and model backends.

item.title: Cardiologent launches multi-agent system for patient-level arrhythmia detection and clinical decision support using ECG and wearable data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Cardiologent presents a multi-agent clinical decision support system that assesses arrhythmias at the patient level, integrating ECG and photoplethysmogram data from wearables to inform urgency and management decisions. The system grounds its analysis in measured features, assembles a comprehensive rhythm profile, and reasons against patient-specific clinical guidelines, with a critic validating each conclusion against cited guidelines. Evaluated against expert cardiologists and a large language model judge, Cardiologent achieved top scores in diagnosis, clinical significance, and management tasks, providing auditable decisions suitable for continuous monitoring applications.

item.title: Researchers release HANDBOOK.md, a benchmark of 65 long-context agentic tasks testing AI adherence to detailed company policies across five domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: HANDBOOK.md is a new benchmark designed to evaluate language-model agents on their ability to follow extensive, binding policy documents over long task horizons, simulating how enterprise employees adhere to company handbooks. The benchmark includes 65 tasks set in fictional company environments with tools like email and calendars, governed by expert-written procedures ranging from 20 to 124 pages across finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, and HR domains. Each task modifies base handbooks to prevent memorization, and grading uses 824 programmatic criteria to ensure agents perform required actions and avoid prohibited ones. Evaluation of thirty model configurations showed the best achieved only a 36.2% pass rate under strict grading, with common failures including ignoring standing policies, acting against required checks, losing rule details over time, and falsely reporting compliance. The researchers have released all tasks, environments, and evaluation tools to support further development in agentic instruction following.

item.title: Researchers propose IMACS framework to separate organization, coordination, and collaboration protocols in multi-agent LLM systems, enabling adaptive protocol selection and organizational design learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce the Intelligent Multi-Agent Collaboration System (IMACS), which decouples three key aspects of multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems: team composition (organization), member alignment (coordination), and the algorithm combining their outputs (collaboration protocol). This separation allows classic organizational theories to be implemented as configurable layers and supports controlled comparisons by varying organizational assignments while holding collaboration protocols fixed. IMACS also enables learning protocol choice per task through Adaptive Org Routing, a meta-protocol that optimizes quality-cost tradeoffs and outperforms fixed protocols in studies using real benchmarks and LLM-judge rewards. The study reveals that accountability placement affects outcomes only when the collaboration protocol routes deliverables through the accountable agent, with optimal placements varying across model families. This finding implies that organizational design in multi-agent LLM systems cannot be hard-coded but must be revalidated or learned for each model configuration, highlighting the importance of adaptable organizational structures in AI collaboration frameworks.

item.title: PatientAgentBench benchmarks patient-facing health AI agents using clinician-validated criteria across 1,200 scenarios, revealing clinical safety and triage gaps in current models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: PatientAgentBench introduces a benchmark framework to evaluate patient-facing health AI agents that interact with simulated patients using healthcare tools. The framework scores conversations across six dimensions with over 100 clinician-grounded criteria, validated by licensed clinicians showing agreement comparable to clinician inter-rater reliability. Testing 10 models across four families on 1,200 scenarios revealed significant gaps in triage quality, clinical safety, and workflow accuracy, with weaker models frequently failing and stronger models still scoring below perfect. The evaluation highlights that current static benchmarks are insufficient for assessing autonomous healthcare agents, as failures emerge only in sustained, tool-using conversations with realistic patient records. The framework is released as a reproducible, clinician-validated standard to help improve the safety and effectiveness of agentic health AI systems.

item.title: AIriskEval-edu Demo launches platform auditing pedagogical risks in educational explanations using GPT-5.5 and fine-tuned Llama 3.1 evaluators [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AIriskEval-edu Demo introduces a platform that audits instructional explanations for pedagogical risks across five dimensions: factual accuracy, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. The platform provides binary decisions, confidence scores, natural-language rationales, and localized evidence spans for detected risks. It integrates GPT-5.5 via API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B evaluator fine-tuned on a K-12 dataset, running on consumer-grade GPUs. The platform operates in AI mode, assessing explanations generated under six simulated teacher profiles, and in human mode, auditing user-written explanations in real time. The local evaluator outperforms GPT-5.5 on most metrics, offering educational institutions a practical tool to audit content within their own infrastructure.

item.title: Researchers find that adaptation site in transformers affects learning patterns and generalization across five objectives using localized LoRA [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated how the location of adaptation within transformer models influences what the models learn, how well that learning generalizes, and how selectively it is applied. They introduced a benchmark covering five objectives-lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, and procedural reasoning-and analyzed each objective's "adaptation geometry" under full-stack and localized low-rank adaptation (LoRA) at early, middle, or late layers. The study found distinct adaptation patterns for each objective, such as lexical binding favoring early-layer adaptation for acquisition and boundedness, while factual association favored later layers, and behavioral learning showed separation between late-layer action acquisition and middle-layer policy gating.

item.title: Researchers propose ClinPRISM, a cost-effective multimodal LLM framework for question answering over irregular clinical time series, achieving state-of-the-art results with low latency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: ClinPRISM is a new multimodal large language model framework designed to handle irregular clinical time series data for question answering tasks. It uses an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder and a temporal evidence distiller to capture and compress sparse clinical evidence into a small number of tokens compatible with a 4-billion-parameter LLM backbone. The model was trained on 30,000 clinical time series paired with multi-scale descriptions and 41,000 instruction-tuning instances across 11 tasks. ClinPRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance on a held-out evaluation benchmark while using only 16 time-series tokens and maintaining an average inference latency of 0.15 seconds per question.

item.title: DocAnnot framework uses GenAI and spatial algorithms to accelerate key information extraction dataset creation with strong auto-annotation performance on CORD and SROIE benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DocAnnot is a new framework designed to speed up the creation of key information extraction (KIE) datasets by combining a Large Vision Language Model for label extraction, OCR for text detection, and a Spatially Informed Contextual Matching algorithm to improve label-value association. Evaluated on CORD and SROIE benchmarks, DocAnnot achieved auto-annotation F1-scores of 0.679 and 0.846 respectively, and models trained solely on its outputs showed respectable performance, though still below human-annotated data. The system automates much of the annotation process, enabling reviewers to efficiently refine outputs and produce near-perfect annotations faster and with less manual effort than traditional methods. This approach offers significant time and cost savings, making it useful for rapid model prototyping and settings with limited resources, while not fully eliminating the need for human intervention.

item.title: Researchers present VLD-RAG, an agentic multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework for multi-page evidence retrieval and reasoning in visually-rich long documents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce VLD-RAG, a framework designed to improve question answering over long, visually-rich documents like reports and manuals by combining text and visual cues across multiple pages. The system builds a multimodal index with text, metadata, and visual data, using a hybrid retrieval strategy that merges keyword-based and semantic searches to identify relevant evidence pages. A coordinated agent workflow involving retrieval, answer, and validation agents enhances evidence coverage and citation accuracy. Evaluation on benchmarks such as LongDocURL and MMLongBench-Doc shows that VLD-RAG outperforms previous vision-based retrieval methods in both evidence retrieval and question answering accuracy, highlighting the importance of agent verification and multimodal hybrid retrieval for reliable grounding when evidence is scattered across pages.

item.title: Researchers test Cognitive Kernel Model to improve behavioral consistency in large language models by enforcing Fact-Heuristic-Emotion state separation across 26 models and 37,403 observations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated the Cognitive Kernel Model (CKM), a prompt-level state-enforcement method that requires large language models (LLMs) to separate input into Fact, Heuristic, and Emotion categories before making decisions. Tested on Korean-language decision scenarios involving ambiguity, ethical conflict, resource allocation, and error handling, CKM was applied across 26 LLMs from four vendors with over 37,000 observations to measure and reduce output variability without changing model weights. The study found that CKM significantly reduced repeated-output variability and decision-flip rates, especially in newer models, with effects not attributable to JSON formatting alone. The approach's benefits increased under sampling stochasticity, and about 45% of the improvement was due to structural scaffolding while 55% came from the Fact/Heuristic/Emotion content. However, CKM did not improve reasoning correctness. Overall, the research shows that behavioral consistency in LLMs is measurable, varies by model, and can be partially improved by enforcing epistemic role separation before decisions.

item.title: Researchers evaluate how text chunk size and number of retrieved segments affect Retrieval-Augmented Generation performance and efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This study examines the impact of text chunk size on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, which enable large language models to retrieve relevant information during text generation. It explores how different chunk sizes-from small segments like sentences to larger ones like chapters-affect generation quality, contextual accuracy, retrieval precision, and computational cost. The research also considers how the number of retrieved chunks interacts with chunk size to influence overall system performance and efficiency. The paper highlights that smaller chunks may improve retrieval precision but limit the information available for coherent responses, while larger chunks provide broader context but can introduce noise and increase computational demands. By systematically comparing these configurations, the study aims to provide insights into optimal document segmentation strategies for enhancing RAG system effectiveness.

item.title: Ontario Power Generation evolves retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for regulatory compliance using Progressive Evidence Acquisition with Cost-Aware Escalation [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Ontario Power Generation developed a multi-stage retrieval pipeline to support regulatory compliance and rate case analysis under Ontario Energy Board requirements, progressing from naive retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to a deep multi-agent architecture with adaptive planning. The final system, called Progressive Evidence Acquisition with Cost-Aware Escalation (PEA-CAE), prioritizes low-cost, high-precision retrieval and escalates to full-document analysis only when justified by expected evidence gain. This approach offers a more practical and cost-effective alternative to domain-specific fine-tuning for large, evolving regulatory document collections. The research highlights how iterative evidence acquisition and adaptive query reformulation are becoming foundational for enterprise-scale question answering systems.

item.title: Researchers find Parkinson's disease selectively impairs motor recovery after typing errors, not error detection, using keystroke dynamics and survival analysis
item.description: Researchers analyzed keystroke data from 57 subjects, including 27 with Parkinson's disease (PD), to distinguish between error monitoring and motor recovery during typing. They found that while pre-error keystroke instability did not correlate with disease severity, post-error recovery time was significantly impaired in PD patients, indicating a selective motor deficit. The study used backspace events as natural error-correction episodes and applied a continuous accelerated failure time survival model to capture recovery time, which outperformed discrete time-to-event models. The dissociation between error detection and motor recovery aligns with electrophysiological evidence that these functions involve distinct neural circuits, with motor adjustment linked to subthalamic nucleus activity. This behavioral difference was detectable through everyday typing and replicated against clinical motor tests.

item.title: Researchers introduce TraceBound diagnostics for adaptive knowledge-graph retrieval, finding that pre-retrieval thinking reduces retrieval quality under open-weight controllers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present TraceBound, a diagnostic protocol for adaptive knowledge-graph retrieval that profiles queries and traces failures to improve inspectability. Their study shows that while TraceBound enhances analysis, it consistently lowers retrieval performance due to repeated and zero-result calls and inefficient exploration budgets. The findings suggest that "thinking before retrieval" should be treated as a control problem in action selection rather than a prompt-format modification.

item.title: Study evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Generation in large language models for digital mental health interventions, measuring its impact on intent detection accuracy and safety within a layered architecture [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers assessed six large language models integrated into the Wysa digital mental health intervention, comparing modes with and without Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to determine its incremental contribution to detecting user intent during volatile situations. The study used anonymized real and synthetic user-chatbot interactions annotated by clinical experts across multiple intent categories such as self-harm and panic, analyzing classification metrics including accuracy, recall, precision, and F1 scores. Findings showed that while RAG increased false alarms, this aligns with safety-critical design principles prioritizing sensitivity by routing flagged cases for further review rather than direct action. The results support RAG as a promising method to enhance the accuracy, consistency, and safety of large language model-driven digital mental health tools.

item.title: Researchers develop Dynamic Multi-Criteria Bottleneck Severity Index (DMBSI) using genetic algorithms to identify and analyze bottlenecks in semiconductor wafer manufacturing with improved accuracy
item.description: Researchers present the Dynamic Multi-Criteria Bottleneck Severity Index (DMBSI), a data-driven method optimized by genetic algorithms to identify the most severe bottlenecks in semiconductor wafer fabrication, which features reentrant process flows and variable conditions. The method analyzes multiple diagnostic signals and rework impacts on cycle time to produce a unified measure of bottleneck severity, validated using Manufacturing Execution System logs from 22 wafer production lots at a Seagate Technology 200 mm fabrication line. The GA-optimized DMBSI achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.80 with observed cycle-time contributions, outperforming expert heuristics and established methods like Theory of Constraints and Value Stream Mapping. The approach also revealed temporal bottleneck migration patterns shifting from dielectric deposition steps early in production to inspection steps later. Counterfactual analysis indicated that reducing waiting time at the top bottleneck step by 50% could lower mean cycle time by 7.2%, with the top five bottlenecks offering a combined potential reduction of about 19%.

item.title: Researchers find EEG foundation models fail to capture long-range temporal correlations, limiting cross-population transfer despite strong spectral feature recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated five EEG foundation models (FMs) to determine if their embeddings retained long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) measured by the detrended-fluctuation-analysis (DFA) exponent of the alpha-band envelope. They tested raw-waveform and spectral-input architectures across multiple out-of-distribution cohorts, comparing recovery of the DFA exponent against the static 1/f aperiodic slope. None of the models represented LRTC effectively; raw-waveform models failed to recover either DFA exponent or 1/f slope, while spectral-input models recovered 1/f slope but not DFA exponent consistently. The study found that classical DFA features could recover the exponent moderately well, and LRTC was orthogonal to the aperiodic slope. Cross-population transfer tests showed limited success, with embeddings dominated by recording-site differences rather than LRTC features, which were more robust across sites. These findings highlight a spectral-temporal dissociation in EEG foundation models that may underlie their fragility when applied across different populations.

item.title: Team swyoo ranks third in ACM RecSys Challenge 2026 with evidence-grounded conversational music recommender separating retrieval and response generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Team swyoo secured third place in the ACM RecSys Challenge 2026 Blind-B industry track by developing a conversational music recommendation system that separates retrieval and response generation to maintain exact entity cues and explanation credibility. Their approach combines hybrid lexical-dense retrieval with fine-tuned Qwen 8B adapters and uses a LightGBM calibration followed by an evidence-grounded propose-assign-select framework for response structuring, achieving second place on the explanation-quality leaderboard. The system's design addresses challenges in traditional conversational recommenders where retrieval and response are entangled, causing loss of precise entity information as dialogue intent evolves. By decoupling these components and structuring generation through explicit evidence assignment, the team demonstrated improved explanation reliability and preserved both catalog cues and fluid user intent in music recommendations.

item.title: Researchers audit molecular representations for human olfaction, finding limited reliability and incremental value beyond conventional chemistry baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a reliability-aware audit of molecular representations used to predict human olfaction, evaluating pretrained encoders like MoLFormer and ChemBERTa against traditional descriptors such as RDKit and Morgan fingerprints. They assessed four claims: global perceptual geometry, incremental predictive value beyond chemistry, cross-dataset replication, and transfer to unseen mixture components, using multiple datasets including Keller-Vosshall, Bierling, and Ma. The study found that human perceptual ratings for intensity, pleasantness, and familiarity are reproducible across participants, but model-human alignment was weak. Learned molecular embeddings did not consistently outperform conventional representations, and MoLFormer showed no clear predictive advantage beyond combined RDKit-Morgan baselines. Cross-dataset agreement was positive but incomplete, and transfer to unseen mixture components showed outcome- and representation-dependent effects with no clear incremental benefit. These results highlight empirical limits of current generic molecular encoders for olfaction and suggest that evaluating representation quality in scientific domains requires separate assessments of reliability, structural alignment, incremental information, replication, and out-of-distribution transfer.

item.title: Researchers propose Dual-purpose Semantic IDs to improve I/O efficiency in large-scale recommendation systems by replacing dense embeddings with discrete tokens [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Dual-purpose Semantic IDs, a method that uses hierarchical quantization to convert continuous embeddings into discrete tokens serving both collaborative identity modeling and content reconstruction. This approach reduces memory usage and system overhead by enabling on-demand embedding reconstruction instead of storing massive dense vectors. The method was validated through offline tests and deployed successfully in production-scale ranking and retrieval systems at a major video sharing platform, demonstrating improved efficiency and content richness in recommendations.

item.title: Researchers introduce GraphRareBench, an auditable benchmark with 2,365 cases and 18,093 target-confounder pairs for phenotype-driven rare disease diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: GraphRareBench is a provenance-preserving benchmark designed to improve transparency in phenotype-driven rare disease diagnosis by including detailed evidence records and graph-defined hard confounders. It contains 2,365 ontology-derived cases and 18,093 target-confounder pairs, with each case featuring a coarsened Human Phenotype Ontology query and a fixed candidate pool. Evaluation on a 237-case gene-component-disjoint test split showed supervised rankers achieving mean reciprocal ranks (MRRs) between 0.640 and 0.740 and target-over-confounder accuracies from 0.898 to 0.916, while agent-based models reached MRRs of 0.746 and 0.718.

item.title: Human Preference aligned Tabular Similarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task-agnostic tabular embeddings are increasingly used for similarity search in real-world business systems such as Product Lifecycle Management (PLM). However, leading embedding approaches are optimized primarily for prediction tasks - not for producing human preference aligned similarity rankings. We argue that standard downstream metrics are insufficient to fully assess embedding trustworthiness for similarity search and that human preference aligned evaluation is a necessary and currently missing component. We present a concrete evaluation procedure and illustrate the problem through a PLM use case.

item.title: Agent Retrieval Bench: Evaluating Repository Context Retrieval for Coding Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24882v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern coding agents are usually evaluated by whether they eventually produce a correct patch, but patch generation depends on an earlier context-acquisition stage: finding the repository files needed for the task. We introduce Agent Retrieval Bench, a file-level benchmark for this upstream retrieval problem. Samples are built from real coding-workflow signals and evaluated against frozen base-commit repositories, with relevance defined by what an agent needs next rather than direct query-file semantic similarity. The benchmark covers four positive-retrieval tasks: code2test, comment2context, trace2code, and edit2ripple; a fifth subset evaluates selective retrieval using natural evidence-backed no-gold cases and counterfactual wrong-repository controls. Agent Retrieval Bench contains 427 samples across 25 repositories: 345 positive examples, 50 natural no-gold examples, and 32 counterfactual controls. The corpus includes 308 base-commit snapshots, 392,000 files, and 7.9 million chunks. We evaluate lexical retrieval, RepoMap, open-source embeddings, selective abstention, and logged agent context selection. No single retrieval family dominates: Qwen3-Embedding-4B has the best sample-weighted MRR on positive samples, Qwen3-Embedding-8B the best Recall@20, and RepoMap the best budgeted context yield at 8K tokens, with task-level winners differing substantially. Selective thresholds calibrated with counterfactual controls do not improve selective success on natural no-gold cases, revealing a calibration gap. Logged trajectories also miss every gold file on 27-35 percent of samples. A controlled seed-intervention pilot finds that retrieval-derived initial context yields higher file F1 with less post-seed exploration than random non-gold context, while oracle gold context shows substantial remaining headroom.

item.title: Eliminating Propagation Delay: Attention-Based Spatial-Temporal Fusion Graph Convolution Network for Traffic Flow Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting traffic flow is crucial to optimizing transportation systems and improving urban mobility. Many graph convolution-based models have been proposed to extract spatial-temporal features and predict traffic flow. However, most focus on spatial-temporal and semantic correlation in topological relationships. There are two primary problems to address. Firstly, the convolutional structure in the model focuses on utilizing static spatial dependencies and spatial-temporal relationships in topological structures, while neglecting the different information propagation delays between adjacent nodes in the convolution. Secondly, these methods often stack a large number of complex structures, resulting in a substantial increase in computational time during the model training phase, thereby disregarding the model's requirements for timeliness. In this paper, we propose a novel network called the Attention-Based Spatial-Temporal Fusion Graph Convolution Network (A-STFGCN). We design a spatial-temporal fusion block to extract the spatial-temporal feature correlations with propagation delay errors removed and to capture both long-term and short-term temporal characteristics of the data within a multi-head self-attention mechanism based on a mask matrix. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves the best overall performance while having good computation and data utilization efficiency compared with the eight baseline methods.

item.title: Mechanisms of Width Scaling in Normalized Residual Networks: The Effective Alignment Dimension [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing theories of neural-network width characterize asymptotic limits, but provide limited guidance on whether an expansion direction identified from finite training data remains beneficial on unseen data. We study this problem for function-preserving residual expansion and introduce the effective alignment dimension, a measurable quantity describing the signal-noise geometry of activation gradients. By deriving the exact mean and variance of the inner product between independently estimated training and test gradients, we obtain a finite-sample upper bound on misalignment probability. The bound depends only on the effective alignment dimension and an effective sample size, requiring finite second moments and a nonzero population gradient, without covariance spectral assumptions or prescribed width-growth rates. We integrate this certificate into the train-test residual-expansion framework, yielding a high-probability condition for test-risk improvement. Experiments across width-controlled LLaMA-style Transformers, Pythia, and ResNet-20 show that wider models exhibit larger effective alignment dimensions and lower empirical misalignment. Direct residual interventions confirm that the alignment statistic predicts the sign and magnitude of held-out loss changes.

item.title: GAUGE: Grading Agent-Built Financial Models Without a Golden Answer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial models combine public disclosures with analyst assumptions to produce forecasts and valuations. While some components can be checked mechanically, forecasts, discount rates, and target prices often admit multiple reasonable answers. Existing benchmarks nevertheless tend to grade such outputs against a single expert reference. Using independently built analyst models for the same companies, we find that across 108 directed pairs covering 65 companies, the median single-reference score is 0.33, 92.6% score below 0.70, and no same-vintage pair agrees on implied price within 10%. Point-tolerance grading can therefore penalize disagreement already present among professionals. We introduce GAUGE, a benchmark for evaluating agent-built valuation models against observed analyst practice rather than a single point answer. GAUGE uses 1,001 vendor-classified analyst workbooks and a 196-task evaluation set, with a three-layer observed-practice envelope, 56 auditable facets, eight validity gates, and deterministic structural checks. We validate the benchmark with a 55-participant known-groups study, company-grouped cross-fitting, and judge-stability audits. On the failure-aware score $\phi_0$, senior analysts average 88.3, juniors 66.0, and finance students 43.2. Across 24 agents and 1,011 scored generations, the best agent scores 53.4, above the student mean but below every senior and most juniors. It passes 93% of mechanical facets and 78% of judgment facets, with a fleet-median gap of 26 points. Current agents are substantially stronger at model construction than valuation judgment. We release the methodology, a gated de-identified data tier, a controlled training split, a versioned 48-task evaluation core, and a withheld refresh pool.

item.title: LLM as Forecasting Planner: Training-Free Text Conditioning for Time-Series Foundation Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-conditioned time-series forecasting predicts a series from both its numerical history and natural-language context, allowing forecasts to account for events and constraints that the past alone cannot reveal. This requires both reliable numerical forecasting and the ability to interpret contextual information. Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide strong numerical forecasts, while large language models (LLMs) can reason over text, but combining their strengths remains challenging because asking an LLM to generate or revise forecast values directly can distort the temporal structure captured by the TSFM. We instead formulate forecasting as a planning problem over TSFM-generated trajectories. The frozen TSFM acts as a simulator that proposes numerical continuations, while the LLM acts as a policy and value function that guides candidate selection and evaluates completed trajectories against the context. We instantiate this as \rc{} (\textbf{L}LM \textbf{A}s \textbf{F}orecasting \textbf{P}lanner), a training-free framework that bridges the modality gap without retraining either model, using Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) over the forecast horizon with a \emph{Ranker} LLM as policy and a \emph{Judge} LLM as value function. Experiments on Context-is-Key and Time-MMD across two TSFM backbones (Chronos and TimesFM) and four LLMs show that \rc{} delivers consistent improvements across model choices, supporting sequential search as an effective training-free approach to text-conditioned forecasting.

item.title: Multiclass Classification without Labels via Posterior Simplex Geometry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many classification problems, reliable instance-level labels are unavailable. However, it is often possible to construct weakly enriched unlabeled samples: datasets selected by different cuts, sources, populations, or experimental conditions that change latent class proportions without revealing them. Classification without Labels (CWoLa) shows that, in the binary case ($K=2$), a classifier trained to distinguish two impure mixtures with different class proportions can recover an optimal class discriminator without knowing the mixture proportions. We extend this principle to multiclass learning from several unlabeled mixtures ($K>2$), where the learner observes only mixture identity and neither latent class labels nor class-prior matrices. We prove that, for a multiclass mixture model, the Bayes-optimal mixture classifier $g^\star$ maps data points into a $(K-1)$-simplex embedded in mixture-posterior space. The $K$ vertices of this simplex are induced by the latent classes through the unknown mixing matrix. Leveraging this geometry, we propose prior-free procedures that train a standard classifier to distinguish mixture identities and then extract latent class structure using either post-hoc simplex fitting or a bottleneck architecture. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Galaxy10 DECaLS show that mixture identity alone can recover latent classes and their fractions in the mixture. By narrowing the gap between weakly supervised and fully supervised performance, we provide a mathematically grounded, scalable tool for multiclass discovery in label-scarce domains.

item.title: Stable FP4 Training via Transposition-Invariant Block Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reducing training precision is a key lever for improving the e ciency of large language model (LLM) training, but pushing beyond FP8 to 4-bit oating point (FP4) remains challenging due to instability during optimization. We identify a fundamental source of this instability in existing microscaling approaches: scale inconsistency induced by tensor transposition. In conventional 1D block quantization, forward and backward passes assign di erent scaling factors to the same values after transposition, leading to biased and unstable gradient updates. To address this issue, we propose a low-precision training framework based on 2D block FP4 quantization, which enforces transposition-invariant scaling and preserves consistency between forward and backward computations. We further combine this with truncation-free scaling and stochastic rounding to control quantization error and maintain unbiased gradients. To handle the sensitivity of attention mechanisms, we adopt MXFP8 quantization for query and key projections, yielding a practical mixed-precision design. We evaluate our method on dense LLMs up to 7B parameters and a 30B Mixture-of-Experts model, trained on up to 100B tokens. Across all settings, our approach achieves stable end-to-end FP4 training and closely matches BF16 performance, with less than 1.3% degradation in perplexity and downstream accuracy. These results demonstrate that enforcing forwardbackward scaling consistency is su cient to enable practical FP4 training at scale, providing a simple and e ective pathway toward more e cient LLM training.

item.title: Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models are increasingly adopted in distributionally robust optimization (DRO), but existing approaches trade off model compatibility and adversarial structure: methods that accept arbitrary samplers do not restrict worst-case laws to a generator family, while generator-parameterized adversaries rely on model-specific access such as likelihoods, scores, or training data. We propose Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization (GDRO), a principled framework that accepts any sampleable conditional generator as the nominal model and restricts worst-case laws to a chosen conditional generator family. The key is the sampler-Sinkhorn pairing: samplers represent the conditional laws exactly, while Sinkhorn divergence compares their induced distributions without likelihood access and can be estimated from samples alone. The resulting population problem admits a direct finite-sample approximation and differentiable primal-dual implementation at the active decision context. For Lipschitz losses, the population Sinkhorn radius bounds downstream degradation. Across explicit and implicit generators, our method reduces rare-context inventory regret by 60% and SocialGAN navigation collisions by 50% relative to nominal decisions.

item.title: Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction and Query for Earthquake Catalogs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24984v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In recent years, the number of events in earthquake catalogs has significantly increased due to the utilization of more effective deep learning based detectors and phase pickers but answering open ended questions such as what characterizes this sequence? remains constrained by rigid spatiotemporal windowing and subjective expert interpretation. We present the first systematic application of graph based retrieval augmented generation GraphRAG directly to raw, tabular catalog records across three independently featured catalogs, a reservoir adjacent swarm, the 2019 Ridgecrest tectonic sequence, and the 2021 Maduo Mw7.4 aftershock sequence. Without the need for manual data structuring, the pipeline builds structurally complete, queryable knowledge graphs for all three. Rigorous evaluation individually verified against catalog derived ground truth and a rule based reference graph exposes failure modes, and four seismology informed prompt fixes eliminate all targeted fabrications while sharply improving mechanism reasoning. A vector RAG baseline demonstrates the graph layers distinctive value, catalog wide summarization and temporal stage comparison. In addition, we have identified two main pitfalls that need attention. GraphRAG thus offers a practical, transferable, near zero cost query interface for earthquake catalogs, where careful prompting ensures the results are consistently accurate and trustworthy.

item.title: Calibrated Partial Resets: Preventing Policy Collapse in Continual Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks are hindered by accumulating dormant neurons and loss of expressivity throughout training, particularly in non-stationary data settings, such as continual supervised and reinforcement learning. Recently, neuron resets have been used to maintain gradient flow and restore plasticity. However, full unit reinitialization often sacrifices peak performance and can destabilize training, leading to policy collapse. To preserve plasticity without destabilizing training, we propose Calibrated Partial Resets (CPR), an optimizer that periodically pulls low-utility neurons toward their initialization, with pull strength scaled by each neuron's utility. Unlike binary reset methods, partial resets avoid brittleness; unlike uniform decay, calibrated utility-scaling concentrates adjustment on the units that need it most. Among compared methods, only CPR avoids policy collapse over 400M training steps in SlipperyAnt, and it outperforms prior decay and reset-based methods on Continual MetaWorld and Continual MinAtar benchmarks. Ablations reveal a tunable trade-off between plasticity and peak performance, highlighting utility-scaled reinitialization as a promising direction for continual learning.

item.title: CogArena: A Multimethod Evaluation of Cognitive Ability Structure in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM cognitive scores are increasingly summarized as per-ability profiles whose dimensions should converge across tasks, respond selectively to matched interventions, and generalize beyond the models used to define them. We introduce CogArena, a procedurally generated 13-paradigm benchmark built around a multimethod framework for determining when cognitive-task scores warrant dimensional labels across five theory-motivated groupings. Across 55 open-weight models, nearly all paradigm correlations are positive and a common axis explains about half the variance. The within-grouping advantage is small, scoring-sensitive, and uncertain across model families. In a separately frozen, fully crossed study across 12 models from six families, targeted scaffolds show a small matched-grouping advantage, but no scaffold-specific contrast survives multiplicity correction and selectivity does not improve held-out-family prediction. The frozen confirmation criterion fails. A post-hoc alternate-wording replication produces a smaller positive estimate and again fails. Together, these results support a boundary conclusion. Theory-aligned prompting produces a small in-battery diagonal tendency, but the present evidence does not establish stable five-dimensional profiles. CogArena provides a workflow joining behavioral signatures, covariance, matched interventions, and out-of-family prediction before cognitive labels are attached to model scores.

item.title: Lantern: Conflict-Aware Gradient Blending for Physics-Guided Diffusion Models in Calorimeter Simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.25060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo simulation of calorimeter showers is a principal bottleneck for the High-Luminosity LHC, and diffusion models have emerged as fast, high-fidelity surrogates. Their denoising objective is purely statistical, however: a model can minimize it while placing the physics wrong. Existing physics-informed generative methods cannot close this gap, because they assume a closed-form law, a governing PDE residual or a hard per-sample constraint, that a shower does not supply: no per-sample PDE governs a stochastic cascade, and energy conservation fixes only one scalar per shower. Standard metrics ignore the correlation structure across calorimeter layers and voxels, comparing showers only in a physics feature space. We address both gaps. We introduce the Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD), a single normalized score for correlation fidelity at layer-wise and voxel-wise scales. We then encode the soft per-sample structure available in a shower as two physics-aware auxiliary losses: a variance-stabilized voxel residual loss grounded in counting statistics, and a graph Laplacian loss over the detector geometry. We combine both with denoising through GradBlend, which anchors the step magnitude to the denoising gradient while letting the auxiliary steer its direction, yielding Lantern, a physics-guided diffusion surrogate. On CaloChallenge Dataset 2, injecting the physics losses through task-symmetric rules such as PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, and ConFIG inflates FPD by 2-100x relative to denoising alone, whereas GradBlend admits the same signal without regression and, with the Laplacian loss, Lantern improves both FPD and CFD. Our ablation on the auxiliary loss scheduler shows that the voxel residual loss, whose gradient conflicts with denoising, requires a terminal denoising-only phase to preserve shower fidelity, whereas the non-conflicting Laplacian loss is insensitive to the schedule.

item.title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: LLM-Based Trace Ranking and Grouped Reward Modeling for Multilingual Numerical Claim Verification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.25069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated verification of numerical claims is a challenging problem, as it requires both language understanding and quantitative reasoning. This paper describes our system for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Task 2, which focuses on ranking reasoning traces generated by large language models (LLMs) and predicting a final verdict for numerical claims in English and Arabic. We explore two approaches. The first approach fine-tunes an LLM-based verifier using LoRA to score each reasoning trace independently as a binary classification problem, and selects the final verdict using Best-of-N selection. We further experiment with adaptive sub-claim decomposition to break complex claims into simpler parts before verification. The second approach uses a lightweight TF-IDF reward model with handcrafted numeric and temporal overlap features to score traces, and aggregates scores by verdict group to determine the final prediction. For Arabic, we compare a general multilingual model against AraBERT, a language-specific model pretrained on Arabic text. Our results show that the LLM-based approach outperforms the lightweight reward model on most metrics, particularly Recall@5, while the reward-based approach shows stronger performance on the Conflicting class. Sub-claim decomposition did not improve performance, suggesting that claim splitting introduces noise rather than aiding reasoning. For Arabic, AraBERT outperforms the multilingual baseline across most metrics.

item.title: Spectral Truncation in Synthetic Control
item.description: arXiv:2607.25074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthetic control (SC) matches a treated unit's pre-treatment trajectory to a weighted combination of donor units. We study Spectral SC, which instead matches the treated unit in coordinates defined by the leading temporal singular vectors of the donor panel, and a hybrid estimator that places separately tunable weight on retained and discarded directions, nesting raw-path SC and truncated Spectral SC as endpoints. We prove that the family reduces exactly to raw-path SC at full rank, that exact balance on $K$ retained dimensions with $N_0$ donors is underdetermined whenever $N_0>K+1$, with an affine solution set of dimension $N_0-K-1$, and that spectral imbalance maps to treatment-effect bias through a finite-sample best-linear-predictor decomposition. We evaluate the estimators across eleven data-generating regimes, using $400$ replications per regime and donor-only placebo validation to select regularization and the mixing weight. Truncated Spectral SC has significantly higher RMSE than tuned raw-path SC in every regime, with paired differences equal to $4$ to $11$ Monte Carlo standard errors. The hybrid estimator selects raw-path matching in most replications and is statistically indistinguishable from tuned SC in most regimes. The result is highly sensitive to preprocessing. With raw inputs, the performance gap is large; after removing unit and time fixed effects before spectral decomposition, as suggested by the assumptions behind our bound, the gap nearly disappears and placebo validation begins to favor truncation. We interpret these findings diagnostically rather than as evidence that Spectral SC should replace raw-path SC. Basis-estimation noise, balancing underdetermination, and fixed-effects contamination determine when spectral matching can help.

item.title: Evaluating Communicative Belief Updates in Large Language Models via Implicature Recognition and Cancellation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.25094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human language is driven by unspoken beliefs and belief updates, making these critical to model for successful communication between large language models (LLMs) and their users. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of LLMs to recognize unspoken beliefs made through implicatures and to understand their updates through implicature cancellation: the pragmatic phenomenon whereby an utterance's implied meaning is weakened or negated. We create the first expert-annotated implicature cancellation dataset, [DatasetName], crowdsourced for human judgements of implicatures and their corresponding cancellations. We find that LLM belief update understanding lags behind that of humans, especially in more naturally-occurring scenarios. Additional control experiments suggest that successes in LLM belief updates may stem in part from a reliance on prior beliefs, and that failures in belief updates may depend on their type and on their form. Overall, our study suggests that current LLMs have not yet reached human-level understanding of unspoken beliefs and belief updates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cesare-spinoso/ImplicatureX.

item.title: OPERA: Offline Policy-guided Expert Routing and Adaptation for Universal Biomedical Image Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.25108v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biomedical image analysis spans diverse modalities and tasks, yet real-world deployment is hindered by severe distribution shifts across scanners, protocols, and patient populations. High-performing models consequently require repeated domain-specific fine-tuning, which is a costly cycle that becomes impractical when labels are scarce or privacy constraints limit data sharing. We propose OPERA (Offline Policy-guided Expert Routing and Adaptation), a multi-agent ensemble framework that addresses this deployment bottleneck by treating expert weight assignment as an offline policy learning problem: a routing policy is learned from a small validation set without gradient updates to any expert agent, then deployed with test-time adaptation to handle distribution shift. OPERA coordinates heterogeneous specialist agents through complementary mechanisms. The expert profiling module learns selection policies offline, enabling informed allocation of expertise. Each agent undergoes confidence calibration through temperature adjustment, ensuring more reliable probabilistic outputs. OPERA also incorporates distribution aware adaptation, where class weights are dynamically adjusted at the batch level using statistics derived from unlabeled test data. Instance level routing assigns each sample to the most suitable expert by leveraging inter model agreement and predictive entropy.
